```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

# Anchor here() to this post so paths work no matter where R starts
here::i_am("posts/welcome/index.qmd")

# House colours, ggplot2 theme, and the packages every post uses
source(here::here("R", "theme_cwr.R"))

# Data download bundle helpers; data_bundle_version is the release version linked at the end.
# Bump it when the data changes and /publish rebuilds the bundle.
source(here::here("R", "data_bundle.R"))
data_bundle_version <- 1

# Post-specific packages go here, and in R/packages.R
library(sf)        # spatial data held as a data frame with a geometry column
library(maptiles)  # fetches web map tiles for a given area
library(tidyterra) # lets ggplot2 draw the tile image that maptiles returns
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data

# Small tidy files produced by R/02_clean_data.R live in data/
districts <- read_sf(here("posts", "welcome", "data", "districts.geojson"))
```

<!-- Opening paragraph: the question this post asks and the one-line answer. -->

## First finding as a plain-language heading

<!-- One or two paragraphs, then one chart. -->

```{r}
#| label: districts
#| output: asis

# ---- The area to draw ------------------------------------------------------
# st_union() dissolves the seven municipal polygons into one, which gives the
# Region's outer boundary without downloading it separately: the shared internal
# borders cancel out and only the outside edge survives.
region <- st_union(districts) |> st_sf()

# The map should show a little of the surrounding countryside, so the Region is
# seen in context rather than floating. This takes the Region's bounding box -
# the smallest rectangle containing it - and pushes each side out by 5% of the
# box's width or height.
bounds <- st_bbox(region)
pad_x <- (bounds$xmax - bounds$xmin) * 0.05
pad_y <- (bounds$ymax - bounds$ymin) * 0.05
bounds[c("xmin", "xmax")] <- c(bounds$xmin - pad_x, bounds$xmax + pad_x)
bounds[c("ymin", "ymax")] <- c(bounds$ymin - pad_y, bounds$ymax + pad_y)

# Everything from here on is drawn in EPSG:3857, the projection web maps use.
# Working in the same projection as the tiles means the streets underneath line
# up with the boundaries on top, with nothing stretched to make them fit.
extent <- st_as_sfc(bounds) |> st_transform(3857)
districts_3857 <- st_transform(districts, 3857)
region_3857 <- st_transform(region, 3857)
frame <- st_bbox(extent)

# ---- The street map underneath ---------------------------------------------
# get_tiles() downloads the OpenStreetMap tiles covering `extent` and stitches
# them into a single image. Zoom 11 is the level where towns, main roads and
# rivers are all drawn but individual streets are not, which is the right amount
# of detail for a map of a whole region.
#
# Tiles are cached in data-raw/ so re-rendering does not fetch them again. The
# finished PNGs in figures/ are committed with the post, so an ordinary site
# render never touches the network at all.
tiles <- get_tiles(
  extent,
  provider = "OpenStreetMap",
  zoom = 11,
  crop = TRUE,
  cachedir = here("posts", "welcome", "data-raw", "tiles")
)

# Everything inside the map frame that is not Waterloo Region. Covering it with
# a translucent white wash leaves the surroundings legible but pushes them back,
# so the eye finds the Region first.
outside <- st_difference(st_as_sfc(frame), st_geometry(region_3857))

# ---- Labels ----------------------------------------------------------------
# 02_clean_data.R worked out where each label should sit: the point furthest
# from any border, so a four-line label has room around it. These nudges move
# some labels off that point, because the three cities are small and crowded
# together in the middle and their labels otherwise collide. Units are metres in
# EPSG:3857, and the numbers come from rendering the map and looking at it.
nudge <- tribble(
  ~district,        ~dx,    ~dy,
  "Kitchener",     -1500,  -1500,
  "Waterloo",       6000,   1500,
  "Cambridge",      1000,  -4000,
  "North Dumfries", 1500,      0,
  "Wilmot",            0,      0,
  "Wellesley",         0,      0,
  "Woolwich",          0,      0
)

labels <- districts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  # Turn the stored label longitude and latitude into points, move them into the
  # map's projection, then keep the result as plain x and y columns, because
  # geom_label() wants numbers rather than geometry.
  st_as_sf(coords = c("label_lon", "label_lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(3857) |>
  (\(points) bind_cols(
    st_drop_geometry(points),
    st_coordinates(points) |> as_tibble() |> set_names(c("x", "y"))
  ))() |>
  left_join(nudge, join_by(district)) |>
  mutate(
    x = x + dx,
    y = y + dy,
    # Four short lines rather than two long ones: a tall narrow label fits
    # inside a city, a wide one does not.
    label = paste0(
      district, "\n",
      label_comma()(population), " people\n",
      label_comma(accuracy = 1)(area_sq_km), " km²\n",
      label_comma(accuracy = 1)(density_per_sq_km), " per km²"
    )
  )

p <- ggplot() +
  # The street map, then the wash over everything outside the Region
  geom_spatraster_rgb(data = tiles, maxcell = 6e6) +
  geom_sf(data = outside, fill = alpha("white", 0.6), colour = NA) +
  # Municipal borders thin, the Region's own boundary thick
  geom_sf(data = districts_3857, fill = NA, colour = dodgerblue, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_sf(data = region_3857, fill = NA, colour = dodgerblue, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_label(
    data = labels, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
    size = label_size * 0.7, lineheight = 1.2, colour = "grey10",
    fill = alpha("white", 0.85), linewidth = 0,
    label.padding = unit(3, "pt"), label.r = unit(2, "pt")
  ) +
  # expand = FALSE keeps the frame exactly where it was put, with no extra
  # margin added around the edges
  coord_sf(
    xlim = c(frame$xmin, frame$xmax),
    ylim = c(frame$ymin, frame$ymax),
    expand = FALSE, crs = 3857
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Title: the finding, in one line",
    subtitle = "Subtitle: what is measured, for whom, and when<br>",
    caption = cwr_caption(
      "Statistics Canada Table 17-10-0155-01 and the 2021 census boundary files<br>Basemap &copy; OpenStreetMap contributors",
      credit = TRUE
    )
  ) +
  # theme_cwr() is built for charts with axes; a map wants none of them. Each
  # element is named individually because the theme sets them individually, and
  # a blanket axis.text would not override the more specific setting.
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_blank(), axis.line.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

# phone_text_scale is below the 0.8 default because seven four-line labels on a
# phone-width map collide at anything larger; 0.7 is where they stay apart and
# stay readable.
cwr_figure(
  p, "fig-districts",
  alt = paste(
    "Street map of Waterloo Region with the borders of its seven municipalities drawn on top.",
    "The three cities sit together in the middle and are densely populated:",
    "Kitchener has 323,917 people on 138 square kilometres, or 2,344 per square kilometre;",
    "Cambridge 165,354 people on 116 square kilometres, 1,431 per square kilometre;",
    "and Waterloo 142,450 people on 65 square kilometres, 2,191 per square kilometre.",
    "The four townships ring the cities and are far emptier:",
    "Woolwich has 31,382 people on 329 square kilometres, or 95 per square kilometre;",
    "Wilmot 22,890 on 266 square kilometres, 86 per square kilometre;",
    "North Dumfries 13,051 on 191 square kilometres, 68 per square kilometre;",
    "and Wellesley 12,413 on 278 square kilometres, 45 per square kilometre."
  ),
  height = 7.4, phone_height = 6.6, phone_text_scale = 0.7
)
```

## Reproducibility and data download

**Reproduce the post**: get the code and data for this post from [`posts/welcome/`](https://github.com/gpberber/chartingwaterlooregion/tree/master/posts/welcome) on GitHub.

**Download the data:** `r cwr_bundle_link("welcome", data_bundle_version)` holds every table used in this post as CSV and Parquet files, an Excel workbook, a data dictionary, and a README with sources and licences. The same dictionary is in the post's [README](https://github.com/gpberber/chartingwaterlooregion/tree/master/posts/welcome#data-dictionary).
